senses.definition: Past tense of will; usually followed by a bare infinitive.

subsenses.definition: Used to form the "anterior future", or "future in the past", indicating a futurity relative to a past time.
examples: On my first day at University, I met the woman who would become my wife.
Hi! I thought I'd come over and introduce myself. My name’s Chema.
I'm really flattered you would call your daughter after me.
They thought anything Elvis did would sell, but that was not true.

examples: When we were younger, we would cycle out to the beach most summer Sundays.

senses.definition: A modal verb, the subjunctive of will; usually followed by a bare infinitive.

subsenses.definition: Used as the auxiliary of the simple conditional modality, indicating a state or action that is conditional on another.
examples: If I won the lottery, I would give half the money to charity.
I'd never do anything that went against my conscience.

quotes.text: If I could fly, I would away to those realms of light and warmth – far, far away in the southern clime[…].

subsenses.definition: Without explicit condition, or with loose or vague implied condition, indicating a hypothetical or imagined state or action.
examples: I would love to come and visit.
Look at that yummy cake! I would eat that all up!
Most other people would do it differently, helping anybody who was in trouble, whether they knew them or not.

quotes.text: It's a piece of old folklore for which I would love to find hard proof.

subsenses.definition: Suggesting conditionality or potentiality in order to express a sense of politeness, tentativeness, indirectness, hesitancy, uncertainty, etc.
examples: I would ask you all to sit down.
I would imagine that they have already left.
I would say/think we would/might do better to catch the earlier flight.

quotes.text: “Those trials are being run by the American army so surely you must have access to the documents?” “Well, yeah, you’d think.”

subsenses.definition: Used to express what the speaker would do in another person's situation, as a means of giving a suggestion or recommendation.
examples: It's disgraceful the way that they've treated you. I would write and complain.

subsenses.definition: Used to express the speaker's belief or assumption.
examples: She looked as if she would be sick.
He's very security-conscious, so he would have remembered to lock the door.
They would be arriving in London round about now.

subsenses.definition: Could naturally be expected to (given the situation, the tendencies of someone's character etc.).
examples: Sorry, officer, I wouldn't know anything about the crime, since I was nowhere near the scene.

quotes.text: The free access model, the media magnate said last week, was "malfunctioning". Well he would, wouldn't he?

subsenses.definition: Used interrogatively to express a polite request; are (you) willing to …?
examples: Would you pass the salt, please?
Just reach me down that file, would you.

subsenses.definition: (chiefly archaic) Might wish (+ verb in past subjunctive); often used in the first person (with or without that) in the sense of "if only".
examples: But as the youth increased their annoyance by declaring that the goddess was quite right, because the Emperor was Archon Eponym of the city of Athens, he said: "Would that he also presided the Panathenaic festival."
